sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None. Every line in this section is yes. One copy problem has no checklist line, but the director may want it:

- **Copy outside the checklist: the times passengers act on are vague, and one sentence is muddled.** This is a defect, weight minor to major depending on whether a timetable sits elsewhere.
  - **The times.** "Between early morning and late evening" (paragraph 1, y≈183) and "the last crossing leaves the quay before dusk" (paragraph 3, y≈487) are times a passenger plans around, and neither gives a clock time. Someone reading this can't tell whether they can catch a 7:00 or a 21:30 boat. In winter they can't tell when "before dusk" is. The text sends them to "printed timetables… in the shelter at each landing", so they only get the real times once they're standing at the landing. The fix is to give the first and last crossing times, the winter last crossing, and the date winter hours begin.
  - **The muddled sentence.** Paragraph 1's last sentence (y≈211–297) runs together two conditions: the tide turning against the boat, and low tide on most mornings. A reader can't tell whether the slower crossing happens whenever the tide turns or on most mornings. The fix is to split it into two sentences and say plainly when the crossing takes longer and by roughly how much.
  - This is common sense, not a sourced rule.

**What's working.**
- **The headline and the purpose.** "Notes for ferry passengers" tells a first-time viewer in one glance what this is and who it's for. Nothing competes with it: there are no images, rules or boxes, and every element on the page carries content.
- **One consistent style.** It uses one typeface, near-black on white, with two sizes. The plain, utilitarian tone suits a public service notice, and nothing looks borrowed from another style.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands on the bold title "Notes for ferry passengers" at top left (about 120–593 px, y 75–115), then drops into the first paragraph and reads down. It looks like a plain informational note or help page for ferry users. It feels calm and clear, though sparse: the text column sits in the left half and the right half is empty. Job (my assumption): a short passenger notice that people scan for when the ferry runs, bikes, and the winter schedule.

What matters first:
- One element clearly dominant: **yes**. The title is roughly twice the body size and bold dark grey; nothing else competes.
- Each level distinct, no near-equal sizes: **yes**. There are only two levels, a title of about 40 px and body of about 19 px, and they are far apart.
- Headings differ in more than size: **yes**. The title is bold and the body is regular.

No lines are `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
None.

Outside the checklist, for the director: below the title there is no hierarchy at all. The three paragraphs cover three separate topics: frequency and crossing time (y 145–310), bicycles (y 340–420) and winter timetable (y 450–530). They have no subheads and no emphasis. The facts a passenger acts on are buried mid-sentence: "every forty minutes", "about twelve minutes", "one boat each hour" and "last crossing leaves … before dusk". Someone scanning for "when is the last boat?" has to read every paragraph. This is common sense and not a checklist defect, so it is minor at this length. The fix would be short run-in labels or bold key times, using weight rather than another size.

**What's working.**
- The title-to-body step is large, about 2×, and weight backs it up (bold against regular). The start point is obvious, and the page has a clean two-level scale with no sizes that nearly collide.
- The title wording names its reader ("ferry passengers"), so the dominant element also says right away what the page is for.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** Also **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas…?**, which comes from the same cause. All the content sits in one block in the top left, from about x 120 to 752 and y 75 to 530 of a 1280 × 800 frame. The right band, about 528 px wide, and the bottom 270 px are empty. The space is gathered into one area rather than scattered, but nothing sits in it and nothing on the page explains it. The page tips up and to the left, so it reads as text dropped into a default template, or a page still loading, rather than a composed notice. Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, "Balance") says a heavy side needs a counterweight. Tschichold and Müller-Brockmann both treat large unexplained empty areas as a fault.
   - **Direction of the fix:** keep the column width, because the measure is right. Then either center the column in the frame, or give the right-hand space a job that counterweights the text. This page has natural candidates: a small timetable, a map of the two landings, or the winter hours set as a side note.
   - **Type and weight:** convention (Arnheim), with a note: a left-set reading column on a wide desktop window is a common web pattern. If this is one view of a responsive page, the cost is mainly that the page looks unfinished, not that it is hard to read. Minor.

**What's working.** Every block hangs from one clean left edge at x≈120, with no near-misses, so the page has a single strong vertical line. The space between paragraphs (≈25–30 px) is one consistent step, clearly larger than the line spacing, so each note reads as its own unit while the three still sit together under the heading.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (weight balances; empty space gathered and deliberate)

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. *Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line and no heading at the foot of a column?* No. The first paragraph ends with "tide." alone on its own line, at about x=120–159, y≈297. The last line is a single short word under five full-width lines. That leaves a notch of white at the foot of the paragraph, and it makes the paragraph look one line taller than it really is. Because the text is a web page, the break will move as the width changes, so this exact runt shows only at this width. Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, §2.4.2, says not to end a paragraph with one short word alone on the last line. Fix: pull "tide." back onto the previous line, or carry two or more words down with it. Ways to do that are `text-wrap: pretty`, a non-breaking space before the last word, a slight change to the measure, or a small edit to the sentence. That sentence is also a very long run-on, and splitting it would solve both problems. Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The body text is set the way reading text should be. It is one plain sans at a comfortable size (looks about 19 px) and near-black on white. Lines run about 62–70 characters, inside Bringhurst's 45–75 range, and the leading looks like about 1.5, which suits that measure. The three short paragraphs read without effort.
- The type plan is economical. One family does all the work, with a bold heading and regular body, and paragraphs are marked by space alone. The heading's weight and size make it the only entry point, with no second face or size competing.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (paragraphs break cleanly, no runts)

Walk (working notes):

First read: the eye lands on the bold headline at top left, then drops into three short paragraphs of body text. It reads as a plain information page for ferry riders. It feels calm and sparse, and the right half is empty. The job, which I'm assuming: give passengers quick, readable service notes on a web page.

Color, 9 lines:
- Small palette: yes. Near-black text on white, with no hues at all.
- Strong color kept to a small share: yes. There is none.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. Dark text on white is close to maximum value contrast, and the structure survives in grayscale.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. There are no temperature cues to get wrong.
- Matching colors look the same: yes. The headline and body look like the same near-black.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colors used for their meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not shown by color alone: yes. There is no color coding.
- Dark theme not pure black: yes. It isn't a dark theme.

No line is no or unsure, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies. The only color is neutral: near-black text on white, with no hue anywhere.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** The near-black text (about 1280 px wide image, text column x≈120–750) sits on plain white. That gives the headline and body near-maximum value contrast, so the text reads easily, and nothing pulls attention away from it. That suits plain passenger notes. The headline and body seem to share one dark tone, so the page doesn't look like two slightly different grays fighting each other.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image has no photo, illustration, icon, logo or mark. It is a text page: a heading and three body paragraphs ("Notes for ferry passengers") in the left column of a 1280 × 800 px frame. The right half is plain white, with no picture and no empty placeholder box. The left column ends near x≈750.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped

**Section.** Charts and data: skipped. The image has no chart, no table of figures and no dashboard. It is a heading and three paragraphs of text. The schedule details ("every forty minutes", "about twelve minutes", "one boat each hour") are written as words in the sentences, not shown as data.

**Findings**
None.
